newsitem.title: USA: Hoffa cries foul as Carey leads in Teamster race.
newsitem.headline: Hoffa cries foul as Carey leads in Teamster race.

text.p: James Hoffa's campaign to head the Teamsters Union accused a court-appointed election officer of irregularities Wednesday as incumbent president Ron Carey took an early lead in the balloting.

Campaign officials for Hoffa, whose father Jimmy Hoffa led the 1.4 million member union in the 1950s and 1960s, filed a protest with Election Officer Barbara Zack Quindel, citing four separate complaints in the counting of some 500,000 mail-in ballots at a rented facility here.
Hoffa aides also complained of what they called the slow pace at which the ballots were being counted.

"Both qualitatively and quantitatively I believe the election officer has failed again to provide the comfort level to this campaign that the process ... should have assured us," said Hoffa campaign manager Tom Pazzi.

With about 12 percent of the ballots tallied by Wednesday evening, the election officer reported that Carey had nearly 58 percent of the vote and was leading Hoffa by 33,441 to 24,432 after counting 65 of the union's 562 locals.

Election observers for the Carey campaign, however, had tallied a total of 122 locals representing more than 21 percent of the vote at the close of counting late Wednesday. Their results gave Carey 54.5 percent of the vote, leading Hoffa by 57,727 to 48,119.
Neither campaign was able to spot predictive trends in the early results, saying the sample was still too small. Ballot- counting is likely to continue all week.

In its protest, the Hoffa campaign said some 20,000 sorted, but uncounted ballots were left in a counting room overnight Tuesday after the night shift of ballot counters stopped work, a violation of Quindel's own rules.
"That's where you steal an election; that's what we were worried about," said Hoffa election observer Dave Robinson, who stayed at his post outside the counting room all night.

The campaign also complained that local-by-local tally sheets did not include the number of challenged and voided ballots, that Quindel had not provided a precise total number of ballots received and that she was deliberately counting Carey-friendly locals first, while skipping Hoffa strongholds.

Although Hoffa has accused the government of favouring Carey, Pazzi did not directly accuse the election officer of rigging the results. But he suggested that selectively counting locals could be used for that purpose.
Quindel denied that ballots were selected on the basis of politics and insisted that there were no breaches in security.
"There is no question in my mind that the ballots are being counted fairly," she told reporters. "Our security is running perfectly, as well as we had anticipated."
The Carey campaign had no complaints.

"At this point, neither candidate has a commanding lead," said Carey spokeswoman Renee Asher. "It is in both of our interests to make sure that this election is fair. We have seen no indication of irregularities."
But other Carey aides said the Hoffa complaints appeared to be a prelude for a post-election challenge if Carey wins.
Hoffa, 55, whose father is presumed to have been murdered by the mob in 1975, has worked for the past three years for a Teamster joint council that was once headed by his father.

Carey, 60, a former United Parcel Service driver and dissident leader of a New York local, is a self-styled reformer who won the union's presidency as the darkhorse candidate in a three-way race in 1991.

The current election is only the second in the 93-year history of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters that has been open to all rank-and-file members. Previous presidents of the union that for years was the symbol of labour corruption were elected by convention delegates.
